UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                          )
    Interconnection of Large Loads to the                 )                      Docket No. RM26-4-000
    Interstate Transmission System                        )

          LIMITED REPLY COMMENTS OF CONSUMERS ENERGY COMPANY

         Consumers Energy Company (“Consumers Energy” or “Company”) respectfully submits

the following reply comments in response to comments filed in the above-captioned proceeding

involving the proposed Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”) addressing the

interconnection of large load customers to the U.S. electric transmission system. 1 Consumers

Energy limits these reply comments to only the jurisdictional issues associated with the proposals

set forth in the ANOPR.2 As Consumers Energy and other commenters explained in their initial

comments, and as the Company reiterates below, the Commission should take care to avoid

asserting the authority to regulate matters that the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) has reserved to the

States. Failure to do so would put the Commission at risk of entangling itself in years of litigation

concerning its authority and hamper the Secretary of Energy’s goal of “ensur[ing] efficient, timely,

and non-discriminatory load interconnections.”3




1
       Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Notice Inviting Comments, Docket No.
RM26-4-000 (Oct. 27, 2025) (unreported) (“ANOPR”).
2
        For avoidance of doubt, although providing only limited reply comments here, Consumers Energy
reserves the right to expand upon these comments and address new and different issues in response to any
formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that the Commission may issue on these matters in the future.
3
        Secretary of Energy, Direction that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Initiate
Rulemaking Procedures and Proposal Regarding the Interconnection of Large Loads Pursuant to the
Secretary’s Authority Under Section 403 of the Department of Energy Organization Act at 2 (Oct. 23, 2025)
( “DOE Directive”).
 I.      REPLY COMMENTS

        “As a federal agency, FERC is a ‘creature of statute,’ having ‘no constitutional or common

law existence or authority, but only those authorities conferred upon it by Congress.’” 4 As a result,

“if there is no statute conferring authority, FERC has none,” and absent “statutory authorization

for its act, [the Commission’s] ‘action is plainly contrary to law and cannot stand.’” 5 To that end,

the FPA makes clear that the Commission’s jurisdiction extends “only to those matters which are

not subject to regulation by the States.”6 To uphold any new Commission regulation, a court “must

determine that it does not regulate retail electricity sales,” which the FPA has reserved as “a job

for the States alone.”7

        Consumers Energy explained in its initial comments why, in light of this statutory

framework and the Supreme Court’s guidance in EPSA, the ANOPR proposal to regulate large

load interconnections to the transmission system is, at best, on shaky jurisdictional ground. A

diverse set of commenters, including public utilities, 8 retail electric regulators,9 and other entities,10

1075, 1081 (D.C. Cir. 2001)).

7

8
         See, e.g., WEC Companies Comments at 3 (“The WEC Companies, like many other utilities with
an obligation to serve their retail customers, are concerned that certain elements of the ANOPR would
ultimately usurp states’ exclusive authority over retail sales . . . .”); DTE Electric Company Comments at 2
(“Extending jurisdiction as proposed in the ANOPR . . . is likely to result in significant and protracted
litigation that would perversely slow investment rather than spur it.”).
9
         See, e.g., California Public Utilities Commission Comments at 3 (“Large load interconnection is
part of retail service and is not part of the transmission system operation or a purchase of wholesale
electricity. Large load customers are end-use retail load customers, and their interconnection and purchase
of electricity is a retail transaction, the terms and conditions of which are subject to state jurisdiction.”);
Louisiana and Mississippi Public Service Commissions Comments at 2-3.
10
        See, e.g., Indiana Energy Association Comments at 4 (“States – including Indiana – have long
regulated the interconnection of retail customers, cost recovery for upgrades, local reliability planning, and


                                                      2
 raised similar concerns.       By contrast, commenters encouraging the Commission to assert

jurisdiction over the interconnection of large loads to the transmission system by and large failed

to meaningfully grapple with the ANOPR’s jurisdictional infirmities.

        For example, certain commenters analogize load interconnections to the generator

interconnection process.11 But unlike generator interconnections, load interconnections involve

the provision of electric service to end-user consumers (i.e., retail customers), making the

generator interconnection process inapposite as a jurisdictional matter. Commenters encouraging

the Commission’s assertion of jurisdiction over large load interconnections likewise err in

asserting that the ANOPR proposal will not interfere with States’ traditional authority over the

provision of retail electricity service because it concerns interconnections to the transmission

system.12    Interconnecting large loads to the transmission system “encompasses more than

transmission service alone,” and “the receipt of energy by large load is inherently tied to retail

distribution and state-regulated functions.” 13 And given the “bright line” that the FPA draws




resource adequacy. These activities fall squarely within the states’ exclusive jurisdiction.”); American
Clean Power Association Comments at 2 (“Load interconnection has historically been a state-jurisdictional
issue, and any Federal action should be measured and carefully considered.”).
11
        See Eolian L.P. Comments at 5; Electric Power Supply Association (“EPSA”) Comments at 8-9.
12
         See, e.g., Vistra Corp. Comments at 6 (“The interconnection of retail loads to the transmission
system is within the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction under sections 201, 205, and 206 of the FPA.”);
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC Comments at 9 (“While the retail sale of energy directly to a load
co-located with a generator at the same point of interconnection is not Commission-jurisdictional, the
transmission of electricity to the co-located load at the shared point of interconnection is Commission-
jurisdictional.”).
13
         Talen Energy Corporation Comments at 5 (“While the ANOPR asserts that the ‘proposal does not
exert jurisdiction over any retail sales to large load,’ it fails to provide sufficient explanation of how the
proposal does not infringe on states’ regulatory authority when its practical result is to determine when and
how retail customers can access power. The act of interconnecting a large load with the transmission system
encompasses more than transmission service alone. As an end use customer, the receipt of energy by large
load is inherently tied to retail distribution and state-regulated functions, and FERC must take care to ensure
that it does not infringe upon those state-jurisdictional areas.”).

                                                      3
 between state and federal jurisdiction,14 comments cautioning against jurisdictional overreach are

well-justified.

        At bottom, the fact remains that the Commission has never asserted jurisdiction over load

interconnections, which inevitably involve the provision of electric service to end-use customers.

The extent of the Commission’s authority to regulate load interconnections is murky at best and

will undoubtedly be the subject of protracted litigation should the Commission decide to move

forward with the ANOPR proposal.15 The Secretary of Energy has rightfully expressed urgency

surrounding the need to establish sound policy to advance the Administration’s goal of

“revitalizing domestic manufacturing and driving American AI innovation, both of which will

require unprecedented and extraordinary quantities of electricity and substantial investment in the

Nation’s interstate transmission system.”16 However, Consumers Energy respectfully submits that

any attempt by the Commission to expand its jurisdictional reach into that reserved to the States

would be a serious and unnecessary misstep that may hamper achievement of the Administration’s

stated goals.

        Finally, should the Commission nonetheless decide to move forward with the ANOPR

proposal to federally regulate large load interconnections despite the jurisdictional issues outlined

above and in numerous initial comments, Consumers Energy respectfully requests that the

Commission limit its assertion of jurisdiction to interconnections to transmission facilities, as

defined by FERC’s longstanding seven-factor test. A diverse array of commenters agree that the


14
        Matthew R. Christiansen & Joshua C. Macey, Long Live the Federal Power Act’s Bright Line, 134
Harv. L. Rev. 1360, 1364 (Feb. 2021).
15
         See, e.g., PPL Companies Comments at 8 (“Whether the Commission can go beyond its traditional
limitations, where it has clear jurisdiction over transmission in interstate commerce and states retain
jurisdiction over the distribution of electricity to end users, is a complex legal question that will likely be
decided by the federal courts.”).
16
        DOE Directive at 2 (citations omitted).

                                                      4
 Commission should continue to rely on its seven-factor test when determining whether a proposed

interconnection concerns a FERC-jurisdictional transmission line or a state-jurisdictional

distribution facility.17 Adopting a new framework, such as a bright-line rule based on voltage 18 or

some other metric,19 would arbitrarily upend decades of Commission precedent—and could have

unintended consequences. In short, the Commission’s seven-factor test should not be cast aside

or revised to bootstrap Commission jurisdiction over large load interconnections.

II.     CONCLUSION

        Consumers Energy respectfully requests that the Commission consider these reply

comments before determining how to implement the DOE Directive.
